# Build where they can watch

The person watches their view while you work. Design as a designer does, in front of them: a rough concept first, then improve it a feature and a part at a time until it is done. Never think out the whole design in silence and show only the end: a finished product that appears at once looks imported, not designed.

- Start at once: this guide and the one example that matches have what you need. Do not read the engine's source, and read at most one example, only the part you need.
- The concept, within the first minute or two: the main parts as simple solids at their real sizes and places (a gear as a plain disc at its pitch diameter, a shaft as a rod), created as the shape and framed (`./ise view frame <name>`). It needs only the main sizes: decide the details (how it prints, clearances, fixings) when you reach each part, not before the concept.
- Build from the inside out, so what you are working on is always in sight: the working parts first (the gears, the board, the mechanism), then what carries them, and what encloses them (a housing, a case, a lid) last. Never put a part over the ones you are about to work on.
- Then improve it one step at a time, running the steps after each so the shape updates in their view. Each run changes one part or adds one feature, never several: the real form of one part (involute teeth on the sun; then the planets; then the ring), a feature (bores, a hub, a lip, fillets), a new part (the carrier; the feet), the clearances. A dozen small updates they watch beat one big one.
- Say each step in a line as you make it ("Concept: housing, ring, sun, three planets at their pitch circles", "Teeth on the sun: 12, module 2"), so the panel reads as the design growing.
- Run the checks once the parts are in (`./ise check`, gears, motion), and fix what they find by updating the parts concerned: the fixes show too.
